paragraphs.text: OF OUR FATHER AMONG THE SAINTS. On the Eternal Existence of the Son and the Spirit with God, and against the Sabellianizers. 1. Judaism is opposed to Hellenism, and neither is pious; both stand outside the truth. After all, the Babylonians also made war on the Egyp-

-tians, and many other impious peoples have opposed other impious peoples. So it is not enough to resist impiety unless the resistance comes from piety. The Jews can say many weighty things against idolaters, and they are right to accuse them of serving the creature rather than the Creator. But they will not be acknowledged as pious merely because they expose impiety. They deny the Son of God, through whom all things came to be, and they charge those who worship the Father through him with polytheism. That is why we have come out from the Greeks and separated ourselves from them, so as not to be mixed up in unclean idolatries. We have also come out from the blasphemy of the Jews: we confess the Son of God and flee the deadly denial of our Lord, who says, "Whoever denies me before men, I will deny him before my Father who is in heaven." We confess the Son as from the Father, as always with the Father, believing him when he says and promises, "Everyone who confesses me before men, I too will confess before my Father who is in heaven." 2. Following this example, we have now also separated ourselves from those who Hellenize under the name of Christianity, who dare to call a work of God God and to worship it. We also separate ourselves from those who Judaize, who corrupt Christianity into Judaism. They deny the God who is from God and speak of one God just as the Jews do. They do not say that he alone is God because he alone is unbegotten and alone the source of Godhead. They say it as though he were barren of a Son and bore no fruit of a living Word and of true [?] Wisdom. For they think that the Word of God is like the word spoken forth [?] from the heart, and his wisdom like the wisdom in a soul. So they say that God together with his Word is one person, just as a man together with his own word is one man. In this they hold nothing more than the Jews, who did not accept the evangelist when he cried out from the very beginning, "In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God." For if God had a Word in his heart that was not truly begotten from him, as God from God, how could the Word be with God,

and how could he be God? A man's word is not a man alongside a man, since it is neither living nor subsisting. It is only a movement of a heart that lives and subsists. As soon as it is spoken it [?] no longer exists, and though it is often spoken it never en[dures]. [?] Seguerianus: "often impious." [?]

[en]dures. But the psalmist [?] cried out long ago about the Word of God, saying, "For ever, O Lord, your Word abides in heaven." In agreement with him, the evangelist confesses that the Word is God. He announces that the Word was made manifest, declares that he came, and proclaims that he became flesh, without including the Father in the Word's becoming flesh. "The Word," he says, "became flesh and dwelt among us, and we beheld his glory, glory as of the Only-begotten from the Father, full of grace and truth." You see that the Word is Only-begotten, that he is manifested in the world and dwells among men, and that his glory is proclaimed as that of the Only-begotten from the Father. It is not as though he himself were the Father, nor as though the Father appeared together with the Word, the way a man [?] appears together with his own word, where the word cannot [?] appear unless the speaker is also present and utters it. Whom, then, do we believe? Those who announce to us a Son who has come to dwell among us from the Father, or those who say that the Father together with the Word is one person? If they are one person, how can one send and the other be sent and be seen through flesh? "No one has ever seen God; the only-begotten Son, who is in the bosom of the Father, he has made him known." Having come, he speaks with his own holy voice, offering the sight of himself and, through that [?], suggesting the knowledge of the Father: "Whoever has seen me has seen the Father." [?] He does not claim that he himself is the Father, for how could anyone see the invisible? He claims that he is such as the Father is. He had said before [?]: "If you had known me, you would have known my Father also." Here he plainly sets out the duality of persons, made known [?] in an undistinguishable [?]... he who is counted worthy to see the Son [?] ... of the Father. For the begetter did not beget something different from himself, but one such as he himself is. So if you think there is only one thing when in truth there are two, you do not know the Father or the Son. Then what share do you have in the Church's teaching? And how will you accept the Master's words, "I and the Father are one"? Again, speaking of the Father, he says, "I am from him, and he sent me." He adds further [?]: "I will ask my Father, and he will give you another Paraclete." For you said flesh [?]. [?]

another. Surely it is plain apostasy to deny the three and to say that he is alone, when he himself says, "I am not alone, for the Father who sent me is with me." He also uses a saying of the Law, and through it he shows that he and the Father are two: "In your Law it is written that the testimony of two men is true. I am the one who bears witness about myself, and the Father who sent me bears witness about me." Look: two persons. If you do not say that they are truly two, then by saying so you do not even allow the testimony to stand as true. For what makes testimony credible is that it comes not from one alone but from two. The Father bore witness from heaven, saying, "This is my beloved Son." The only-begotten Son bears witness that he is the Son of God, and he plainly spoke with the Father in the hearing of men, saying, "I thank you, Father, Lord of heaven and earth, because you have hidden these things from the wise and understanding and revealed them to little children. Yes, Father, for such was your good pleasure. All things have been handed over to me by my Father." What answer do the servants of the Jews' denial give to this? They contrive [?] to avoid being plainly refuted by the Gospels of our Lord Jesus Christ. Do they say that two hypostases appear here in such a way that one, the Father, is God, and the other, the Son, is a man? Alas for the impiety! How does this differ from the denial of the Samosatene? Let them tell us how a man could dare to say of himself, "Whoever has seen me has seen the Father." And how could the evangelist testify that he spoke these things of himself, that he called God his own Father, making himself equal to God? No man is equal to God. But the God who is from God will have equality by nature with the one who begot him. Paul testifies to this too, describing not the incarnation but what came before the incarnation: "Who, being in the form of God, did not regard being equal with God as something to be grasped." We know that the Saviour often spoke in a human way too, but not when he says, "I am the one who bears witness about myself, and the Father who sent me bears witness about me." For it is not a man who was sent into the world and who says, "I came forth from the Father and have come." And: "For God so loved the world that he gave his only-begotten Son, so that everyone who believes in him may not perish but have eternal life." And it is he who says, "I have come down from heaven, not to do my own will, but the will of him who sent me." But if you want to hear him

Man was made according to the likeness of God, and man is not God. What is like something is not that very thing; it is only made like it. Similarly, the kingdom of heaven is like a net and like a seed, yet the kingdom of heaven is none of these. And one who has been made a disciple for the kingdom of heaven is like a householder, but he is not a householder. There are many other cases of this kind. Among bodies too there are likenesses: a wolf is like a dog but is not a dog; tin is like silver but is not silver; bronze is like gold but is not gold; scarlet is like blood but is not blood; gypsum is like snow but is not snow. Many other such things can be observed. So the Son is not like God, for he is God; rather, he is one with him, as it is written: "I and the Father are one." He interpreted the oneness as Godhead, and not a Godhead like that of those who have been deified. He in fact sets it against that kind, as the saying of the Lord shows. For he is God, not in the way a man is, who was made according to the likeness of God and is called a god by likeness, not by nature. Such a man has an essence that has been made like God and that even advances in that likeness. By this nature we are already "children of God," and "when he appears, we shall be like him." But where the essence is the same, essence does not advance to more or less. Rather, a man [?] ... [Textual notes:] "and like ... the kingdom of heaven," and the last phrase, "the kingdom of heaven is ... of them," are missing in the edition. ... "and many other such various things," but "various" is absent in [?] the same. "Against the Homoousion." Edition: "On the Homoousion."

speak in a human way, in keeping with the form seen in the flesh and with what his hearers took to be bare humanity, listen to him saying, "If I bear witness about myself, my testimony is not true." He means that a man who bears witness to himself is not trustworthy and is not thought to be. But he also says, "Even if I bear witness about myself, my testimony is true, for I know where I come from and where I am going." When he counts the Father and himself together and says there are two witnesses to his glory, he is not saying human things. He is speaking beyond all human dignity. And why do I say human? Beyond the angelic, beyond principalities, beyond powers, beyond dominions. For how can man be counted together with God? What nearness or what fellowship is there between them? But when he says, "I thank you, Father, Lord of heaven and earth," does he seem to you to be a man? Rightly so, for the Godhead that came into the world has the human mingled with it. 4. But do not let the veil of the flesh keep you from recognizing God. He immediately goes on to say of himself: "No one knows the Son except the Father, and no one knows the Father except the Son and anyone to whom the Son chooses to reveal him. Come to me, all you who labour and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest. Take my yoke upon you and learn from me, for I am gentle and lowly in heart, and you will find rest for your souls. For my yoke is kind, and my burden is light." The Lord has shut the door on your slander. He shows that he is God: even in human form he is known by the Father alone, he knows the Father, and he reveals the knowledge of himself and of the Father to those found worthy. He calls us to himself, promises rest with himself, and urges us to carry his yoke. By saying this he unveils the Godhead. He discloses the surpassing greatness hidden by the lowly form and displays the heavenly authority curtained by an earthly body. Why should I list the countless divine sayings of our Lord Jesus Christ? Through them the Samosatene's innovation about the Saviour, that he was a mere man, is rightly cast out, and with it the senseless babble of those who imitate him. Come, let us recall just a few testimonies. Who is it that says such things as, "Not everyone who says to me, 'Lord, Lord,' will enter the kingdom of heaven"? This is not the word of a man but of God,

[?] who knows his genuine birth from the Father and for that reason does not refuse to be called Lord in the proper sense. For one begotten of the only Lord is Lord, as Moses also says: "The Lord rained sulphur and fire from the Lord." At another time the Saviour says to the apostles, "You call me Teacher and Lord, and you are right, for so I am." And again he shows that he is master of his Father's house, as the only-begotten Son: "If they called the master of the house Beelzebul, how much more those of his household!" So it is clear to everyone that Jesus Christ, the Lord of all, is God, since he is begotten from God. And having said, "Not everyone who says to me, 'Lord, Lord,' will enter [?] the kingdom of heaven," he adds words that plainly make the Father known to us: "but the one who does the will of my Father in heaven." 5. So you have a Son, and you have a Father. Do not be afraid of the duality, for it is not divided in nature. Whoever speaks of the two has not separated the offspring from the begetter. Nor should we shrink from speaking of two because of the opposite madness of those who denied that the Godhead of the two is one. There is one God, because the Father is also one. But the Son too is God, and he has identity with the Father as a Son with his Father. He is not himself the Father, but he is united to the Father in nature. They are two in number but one perfect essence: two, but not made of two parts. The perfect Son comes from the perfect Father, one who is from one who is, the imprint of the Father's hypostasis. He is not a word without subsistence but a living power and the cause of life for all things. He is not like a man's power, by which a man is powerful, for a man's offspring or son is not his power. But the Son of God is his power. So the Father is perfectly powerful, because he is the Father of the Power, and the Son is perfect power, because he is his offspring. The Son is also the wisdom of the Father, not like a man's wisdom, by which a man is wise, but wisdom from the wise. Of him it is said, "To the only wise God through Jesus Christ, to whom be glory for ever. Amen." "But the Father did not beget." Then how is he Father, and of whom? And if he did beget, the one begotten exists. "I too," he says, "confess a begetting, for the word is begotten when it is spoken and known." Then tell me, how many times will the same one be begotten? Or will you say that many Words of God are begotten each time? Will you picture God as sometimes silent and sometimes speaking, changing from silence to speech with opening lips or a moving heart? God is not a man. "You thought, lawless one, that God would be like you?" O man, even if you hear of God's eyes, or of his other bodily members,

do not think of them in a fleshly way. Use the likeness of bodily things to understand what is bodiless. For you have been told, "God is spirit." In the same way the Word is not human, nor is he like your word. He is God, even if you do not think so. Yet there are not two Gods, since there are not two Fathers either, and the one begotten is not of a different essence from the one who begot him. 6. Whoever introduces two first principles proclaims two Gods. That is Marcion's impiety: he speaks of a just God, Father of his own Christ, and another, good God, Father of his own Christ. Again, whoever says that God is unoriginate and another God is originate also speaks of two Gods, because of the difference of essence that he blasphemously introduces. But where there is one first principle and one offspring from it, a most exact and natural image, since it was also begotten [?] from him, there is one God. The Godhead is conceived as perfect in the Father, and the Father's Godhead also exists perfect in the Son. You can grasp what is meant even through this small example, which divine Scripture has given when it names Christ the image of the invisible God. Here again let us avoid what is unlike in the example, namely that an image is the work of a craftsman and of a different essence. Instead let us confess that the image of God is begotten and consubstantial. Even so, whoever sees the image of the king sees the king and says, "Look, this is the king." He has not made two kings, nor made the image a part of the king or the king a part of the image. In the same way, then, the Father is one God, and there is one Godhead of Father and Son. But on your account the one God will be a compound of two imperfect parts. Against this impiety it is good to stop one's ears and wash one's soul clean. Whoever imagines this confesses neither the Son nor the Father, since neither Father nor Son can be conceived as imperfect. 7. "But it is written," he says, "'I am in the Father, and the Father is in me.'" Yet the Father is not a word in the Son's heart. Neither, then, is the Son a word in the Father's heart. He is the living Word from the living God the Father, made manifest by eternal begetting and existing with the Father without beginning, so that the Father is never conceived of as alone. For the Trinity is always a Trinity and receives no addition of Godhead. Nor [?] what did not exist before, with [?] ... (Seguer., Gobler. and Felc.: "begotten.")

[es]sence, nor power did he number with him. Things that are not eternal cannot be counted together with the eternal, and things that do not share in Godhead are not ranked with the Godhead. How, then, is the begotten in the begetter, and the begetter in turn in the begotten? How is this one in that one, and that one in this? Because the one is such as the other is, and the other such as the one is. So the two are also one: the Son does not differ, is not cut off, and is not conceived as having another form or a foreign character. He is God, just as the Father is. When he said, "I and the Father are one," the Jews were indignant and said, "Because you, being a man, make yourself God." The Saviour answered by confirming what they had said, as though he had meant nothing other than this when he said, "I and the Father are one": that he too is God, being the Son of God. "If he called them gods to whom the word of God came, and Scripture cannot be broken, do you say of him whom the Father sanctified and sent into the world, 'You are blaspheming,' because I said, 'I am the Son of God'? If I am not doing the works of my Father, do not believe me. But if I am doing them, even though you will not believe me, believe the works, so that you may know and understand that I am in the Father and the Father is in me." So the Son being in the Father and the Father in the Son means this and nothing else: that the Son of God is the one begotten from God, God by nature, what the Father is, showing the Father's form in himself and being shown in the Father's hypostasis. 8. So there is one, and one, and the duality is not [?] in nature, since it lacks nothing in perfection. The Father, as Father, is the whole fullness of the Godhead, and the Son, as Son, is the whole fullness of the Godhead. For through both one form is conceived, shown wholly in both. Let no one deny the life that was manifested in the world: "which was," he says, "with the Father and was manifested to us." Even before it was manifested, it was what it was seen to be when it was manifested. For it is begotten eternally and exists with its own Father. Let no one imagine that by denying the three he finds the unity. Let him rather conceive the one in the Trinity, holding the sum of the faith in baptism and in the three holy seals through which he has been born again to salvation. Let him remember the Apostle, who says, "One God the Father, from whom are all things, and one Lord Jesus Christ, through whom are all things." Let him remember the Father, who says, "From the womb, before the morning star, I begot you." And let him remember the Son, who testifies that he was with the Father before the world, having the glory of the Godhead: "Glorify me," he says, ... (21 Seguerianus: "to be of God" ... "of the truth" ... "of the Apostle saying to us.")

"Father, glorify me with yourself with the glory which I had with you before the world existed." He asks for the glory that belongs to him as man, while testifying that he had the glory that belongs to him as God before the world. He had the glory because he was and existed, for what does not exist has never been glorified. And if he existed, he had also been begotten, for there is no son who has not been begotten. "But if he has been begotten," says the objector, "he is outside the one who begot him, and has been divided off. Yet the Word, since he is in God, must be undivided and must not appear outside God. For where could he appear outside, since God has filled all things, as it is written: 'I fill heaven and earth, says the Lord'?" 9. With fancies like these they try to do away with the generation of the Son, his eternal procession from the Father, his existence with the Father, and the truth that the Father subsists perfectly in himself and the Son also subsists perfectly in himself. Let them learn, then, that they understand neither what they are saying nor the things about which they make confident assertions. They confine God to a place, and then imagine the Son in another place, and suppose that the two have been parted, one there and the other here, if the Son is confessed to have been begotten and to have come forth from the Father as himself. "What is the place of my rest?" says God through the prophet. "Heaven and the heaven of heaven will not be enough for you," Solomon says to God. With the strongest proof God convinces people that no place can contain him: "For my hand," he says, "made all these things." So the things that were made do not contain their maker, who existed even before them, who gives them their being, and on whose power they are supported. That is why Paul says: "From whom are all things, and through whom are all things, and to whom are all things"; and again: "For in him we live and move and have our being." 10. So when you think about God, the Word and the Spirit, put away for me the idea of one fixed in a place. Put away separations of place, and do not suspect that the Father, being in one place, sends the Son out somewhere else by begetting him. These false, or rather godless, reasonings are what trip you up concerning the existence of the Son. And together with the Son you have also denied the Holy Spirit, through the ... by one ... [?] ... he says. (25) Seguerianus: γεγενημένος.

... the water in his hand, and all the earth in his grasp. Since all things are so very small to him, as the prophet's comparison modestly suggests, how could he be thought to be stretched out to match a small and very little creation? God has not filled all things by being stretched out alongside them all. That would be something bodily, as if one were to say that the air has filled the space between earth and heaven. Rather, as power he holds all things together, for power is incorporeal and invisible; it neither encircles nor is encircled. The same is true of the Son and of the Holy Spirit, for it is through the Son and in the Spirit that God both established all things and, holding them together, preserves them. It is impious, then, even to ask or to imagine where God is, or what place the Word has been given, or what dwelling the Spirit has been allotted. If anyone should say that the Son does not exist and has not been begotten because the place of his being can be neither conceived nor found, such a person would have to say that the Father does not exist at all, and that there is no God, since no place of God can be found either. "The fool has said in his heart, 'There is no God.'" Fools indeed are such people, deceiving themselves with empty fancies. These are the words of infants and of the utterly senseless, who want what is incorporeal to be seized by the eye and enclosed in a place. 11. Let us offer them some brief images drawn from incorporeal things within our reach, recalling certain things that exist among us and are seen in creation, in case by climbing up through them they might somehow conceive the incorporeality of the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit, and no longer imagine places for them or think up local divisions of the Trinity. The law, being incorporeal and spiritual, is in the mind of one who has learned the law. In that same mind are also the prophets, the Gospels and the apostles. So it is said concerning the words of the law and the prophets: "They have Moses and the prophets." And the Saviour says that the one who has old and new words in his mind is like a householder who brings out of his treasure things new and old. The mind of Moses received all the wisdom of Egypt, as well as the wisdom given him by God. And Daniel, having received all the learning of the Chaldeans, also held the manifold thoughts of divine wisdom, which God indicates through Ezekiel: "Are you wiser than Daniel? Has not every secret been shown to you?" Solomon's understanding was beyond counting, and the breadth of his heart ... [?] the prophetic comparison modestly shows ... [?] sand; Seguerianus adds φησίν.

... like the sand by the sea. When they see so great a multitude of wisdoms gathered in one mind, let them consider that these are not in a place. For how large would a man have had to grow to be able to hold so many, if he kept each of his contemplations in a separate place? Since, then, spiritual things here below do not need more places when there are more of them, but revolve around one and the same mind, let us think also of the things above us, which are incorporeal in themselves, the Father, the Son and the Spirit, as neither needing places nor divided by places. And let no one dare, on that account, to suppose that the Father, or the Son, or the Holy Spirit does not exist, simply because one cannot mark off and assign a place to each. The Father exists, having perfect and unfailing being, the root and source of the Son and the Spirit. The Son exists in the fullness of the Godhead, the living Word, the offspring of the Father, lacking nothing. And the Spirit of the Son is also full, not a part of another, but whole in himself. And so the Trinity, which truly exists, is joined without any gap. For nothing divides them; they are together always [?], since no age falls between them. It displays one and the same form, the Father being seen in the Son, and the Son being both perceived and shared in the Spirit by man. "For we all," he says, "with unveiled face beholding as in a mirror the glory of the Lord, are being transformed into the same image from glory to glory, as from the Lord who is the Spirit." 12. Let us not, then, imagine three indivisible parts, as though they were bodies. That reasoning is impious and foreign to perfect incorporeal beings. Let us accept an undivided union of being among those who are with one another without any gap; and while three truly subsist, let us conceive one form, beginning from the Father, shining in the Son, and made manifest through the Spirit. This is why those who bear the Spirit bear Christ. "For if anyone," he says, "does not have the Spirit of Christ, he does not belong to him. If Christ is in you, the body is dead because of sin," and so on. And John says: "By this we know that he is in us, by the Spirit whom he has given us." Paul calls our bodies a temple of the Holy Spirit, yet he says that Christ is in us. And when Christ dwells in our inner man, as it is written, it is God who dwells in us: "For do you not know," he says, "that you are God's temple, and that the Spirit of God dwells in you?" In this way, learn reverently from the divine words that the Godhead is indivisible, perceiving one form in three, not composing one thing out of three. (40) Seguerianus: στρέφεται.

And let us see them as inseparable in what they do as well, listening to the Apostle as he leads us into the mystery and says: "There are varieties of gifts, but the same Spirit; and there are varieties of service, and the same Lord; and there are varieties of working, but it is the same God who works all things in all." And after listing the gifts he adds: "All these are worked by one and the same Spirit, who distributes to each individually as he wills." When all things are worked by God through Christ in the Holy Spirit, I see a single, inseparable working of the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit. 13. But I do not, on this account, run together the "from whom," the "through whom" and the "in whom," and force the Trinity into a single unit. Nor do I suppose that God is composed of three, as man is composed of spirit, soul and body, which is what those people dare to say; nor do I give up their inseparability to so impious a notion. Nor do I accept it if someone says that the Son and the Spirit are inseparable from the Father in the way that the inner word, or the spoken word, is inseparable from the one who thinks and speaks. For the parts of what is composite, and the motions of what is moved, have nothing in common with a nature that is uncompounded and unchangeable. Besides, how could the Father be sending a part or a motion of himself when he sends the Son? Or the Son, when he sends the Holy Spirit into the world? Or was the Son not sent by the Father? He testifies to it everywhere; he promises to send the Spirit, the Paraclete; and he does indeed send him, as he promised. But those who turn the Trinity into a single unit try to falsify the sending, just as they do the generation. They say that the Son, being within the Father, works the sanctification of a man; that is, the one and only God himself works it, and in this way it was the man who was sent, not God from God. "For how," they say, "was the Word sent, if he is not divided or separated from the one whose Word he is?" Yet who would deny that the incarnation of the Word has been proclaimed, when the evangelist cries out, "The Word became flesh," and the Saviour himself declared, not once but many times, that he had come down from heaven? Indeed the apostle Paul insists to the Galatians that our Lord Jesus Christ is not a man. And even if he bears the same name of man as we do, he is the second man, not like the first, earthborn one; the one became a living soul, the other a life-giving Spirit. Goblerianus and [?]: καὶ καταλλάξας τὰ χαρίσματα. (46) [?]: ἐνεργεῖται.

14. For these divine and apostolic words and teachings, and his works too, bear witness to his Godhead, done as they were with heavenly authority: when he commands the elements, rebukes spirits, restores the disabled by his power, and heals diseases by his will; when he speaks openly of his authority and does not hide it; when death is abolished through him, and life and incorruption are brought to light; when the corrupted nature of humankind is created a second time, and the world is renewed through his coming, and a new creation appears through the resurrection of Christ, the body of our humiliation being transformed to share the form of the body of his glory, and the whole creation being set free from the bondage of corruption into the freedom of the glory of the children of God. That our incarnate Lord and God Jesus Christ is not the Father, nor, as they would say, the only God, all the divine Scriptures bear witness. They proclaim that the one who came is the Son of God, and they show him always speaking of the Father, saying that he came from the Father and is going to the Father. There is no need to make this long by citing testimonies, for practically all the Gospels and the writings of the apostles point to this. 15. They raise other objections against us taken from the Greeks, and bring in the blasphemies of the Jews, mocking the mystery of the sending and the incarnation of the Word. "For if he is sent and comes down," they say, "he will not be with the one who sends him, nor will he be together with the one who remains above." Let them learn not to understand "above" and "on high" in a merely bodily sense, but to think of something more profound. For "The Lord is high above all nations," and "I will exalt you, O Lord," and "Praised and highly exalted forever" do not present the Lord as being in some place up aloft, nor do they depict God as being lifted up by men, or by the other beings who sing his praises; they speak of the majestic height of the invisible Godhead. And the one who says, "The heaven of heaven belongs to the Lord, but the earth he has given to the children of men," is not allotting heaven to the Lord as a dwelling place and the earth to men; he is showing the supremacy and majesty of God. So when what is venerable and majestic is called heavenly, and in contrast to it what is lowly ... (55) [?]: φάσκοντες. Shortly after, in the edition ...

... [?] humbled himself. So let no one bring forward the bodily expressions, that is, "descent" and "sending," to deny his incarnation, on the grounds that God does not come down in a local sense and is not sent. Rather, let them listen to the Apostle explaining the matter, and the comparisons that go with it, when he says: "Who, being in the form of God, did not regard equality with God as something to be seized, but emptied himself, taking the form of a servant, being made in the likeness of men." This was the descent; this was the sending into a garment lowlier than his dignity: a stepping down, the putting on of human form, carried out according to the will of the Father. And if the Word is not confined by place or body, he will not be torn away from the incorporeal Father by being united with a body. For the body received him because he willed it, insofar as fleshly nature was able to receive God. Yet he remains in his own nature no less than he did before the incarnation. So his descent from heaven was not a departure from heaven, nor was his sending a separation from the Father who sent him.
